metric.hidden_semantic_cost.basis: all-fragments (Go only; this worker is scoped to a single language shard per Task Packet 'Assigned languages: Go'). Common-basis reconciliation across all ten languages is performed by the runner once all language shards for this metric are merged.
metric.hidden_semantic_cost.exclusions_applied: Per checklist instruction, a behavior is not counted as hidden where the fixed local syntax makes it unambiguous under the Go language specification (e.g. explicit pointer dereference &x/*p, explicit (int, error) multi-return, explicit if err != nil, explicit defer keyword, explicit sync.Mutex/atomic use) — these were scored 0 hidden-cost units for their respective probes.
metric.hidden_semantic_cost.methodology: Frozen checklist per semantic_compression.md Section D: implicit conversions (IC), hidden writable aliasing/mutation (HA), overload/dynamic dispatch not locally evident (OD), implicit allocation/copy/move/destroy/cleanup (IA), implicit exception/failure propagation (IE), hidden nullability/optionality (HN), implicit representation change (IR), context-dependent overflow/numeric behavior (CO), hidden side effects on existing state (SE). For each of the 44 frozen probes (capability_universe.json), the idiomatic Go fragment (R1-R10 authoring rules) was itemized for occurrences of these 9 categories that are NOT locally unambiguous under the Go language specification (per the instruction 'do not count a behavior as hidden if the fixed local syntax makes that behavior unambiguous'). Per-probe hidden-cost unit counts were summed and averaged, then normalized to a 0-100 scale where 100 = zero hidden-cost units observed and 0 = the theoretical maximum of 9 hidden-cost categories triggered on every probe (higher = better, i.e. fewer hidden behaviors).
metric.hidden_semantic_cost.not_double_counted_note: Each underlying rule was counted once per probe under its single most-applicable checklist letter, consistent with the instruction not to count the same underlying rule twice across descriptive categories within one metric.

F02.P1.note: var v int32 without initializer is auto zero-initialized by the language; the fixed declaration syntax does not signal whether the zero value or a later assignment is the value a reader should rely on before the branch runs.

F02.P2.note: Go has no documented way to obtain genuinely uninitialized bulk storage; array/slice acquisition always implicitly zero-fills, which is an implicit allocation/initialization behavior not visible at the acquisition syntax (R9 substitution).

F03.P1.note: x++ wraps silently on signed overflow; Go provides no checked-arithmetic mode, so the overflow behavior is not signaled by the plain operator.

F04.P2.note: A Go slice re-slice/view shares the header-vs-backing-array split; whether elements are copied or shared is not evident from the plain slicing syntax without documentation knowledge.

F05.P1.note: Passing a slice by bare value f(x) copies the slice header but aliases the backing array; the ordinary call site gives no local signal that element writes propagate to the caller.

F05.P3.note: Go closures capture enclosing locals by reference implicitly; the capture-by-reference aliasing is not visible at the closure literal's use site.

F07.P1.note: a*b+c on int32 wraps silently on overflow with no local signal.

F07.P2.note: Integer division truncates toward zero and remainder sign follows the dividend; this rounding/sign rule is implicit in the plain / and % operators.

F08.P1.note: Go has no checked/saturating/wrapping-named integer operations in the standard library for this case; the plain + operator's wrap-on-overflow behavior is the only rung available and is not locally signaled.

F08.P2.note: Integer division by zero triggers a runtime panic (implicit failure propagation via panic/recover machinery) with numeric-edge behavior not visible at the / operator.

F10.P1.note: Explicit int32(big) narrowing conversion truncates silently on overflow with no error/trap signaled by the conversion syntax.

F11.P1.note: Out-of-range indexed read panics at runtime; the plain xs[i] syntax gives no local signal of the possible failure.

F11.P2.note: A Go sub-slice shares the backing array with the original; writes through either are mutually visible, which is not evident from the slicing syntax alone without documentation knowledge.

F12.P1.note: Go has no native Optional type; a *int or a sentinel value stands in for absence (R9 substitution), and the pointer's dual use as 'value or absence' is a hidden nullability concern at every dereference site.

F12.P2.note: No optional-aware chaining/mapping operation exists in the standard library; the explicit nil-check substitute still carries the hidden-nullability cost of the underlying pointer representation (R9 substitution).

F14.P1.note: Go has no closed sum/variant type; an interface-based substitute (R9) leaves the alternative set open to extension from any package, which is a hidden departure from the closedness the canonical task names.

F14.P2.note: A type-switch over an interface has no compiler-enforced exhaustiveness; an unhandled concrete type silently falls through the switch (implicit failure to signal) and the dispatch set itself is open (not locally evident which concrete types exist).

F14.P3.note: Extending behavior via a new type implementing the interface from a separate package is resolved by runtime dynamic dispatch through the interface value; the concrete implementation reached is not evident at the call site.

F15.P3.note: A slice of an interface type dispatches tag() to the concrete type at runtime; the concrete type is erased from the declared element type and not locally recoverable.

F16.P1.note: append() on a growable slice may silently reallocate and copy the backing array when capacity is exceeded; the plain call site gives no local signal of whether reallocation occurred.

F16.P2.note: Go map iteration order is intentionally randomized by the runtime (a context-dependent/nondeterministic behavior not visible at the range statement), and an absent-key lookup silently yields the zero value rather than signaling absence unless the two-result form is used.

F17.P2.note: Go has no deterministic end-of-lifetime hook (finalizers are explicitly documented as unreliable/best-effort); the nearest substitute relies on an explicit scoped Close() convention rather than a language-guaranteed hook (R9 substitution), leaving the true GC-driven lifetime implicit.

F18.P2.note: Export/visibility is encoded implicitly via identifier capitalization convention rather than an explicit visibility keyword, so the exported/unexported status of a name is a representation fact carried only by its spelling.

F19.P1.note: A goroutine's stack/scheduling resource is implicitly allocated and managed by the Go runtime with no explicit resource-acquisition syntax at the `go` statement.

F20.P1.note: cgo's `import "C"` pseudo-package crosses into C representation/ABI concerns (calling convention, cgo-generated shims) that are not visible in the Go-side call syntax.

F20.P2.note: The `//export` cgo directive triggers an implicit additional cgo build/codegen step whose artifacts and C-ABI wrapper generation are not visible in the exported function's Go source.
